title: CGC — THE THRESHOLD
model_settings_policy: Inspect the installed model and export its settings; this JSON is a creative manifest, not an importable app queue.
reference_assets: Three full assets are embedded in this HTML. Use the download buttons or parse img data URLs. Do not send the storyboard sheet to image-to-video.

shots.title: The line becomes glass
shots.purpose: Hook the viewer with a real material detail. It should take a moment to recognize the object, then become unmistakably a glass edge. Do not begin with a generic empty black screen.
shots.start: Extreme macro. One polished glass edge sits near x=58%, almost vertical, running from y=15% to y=88%. A graphite mullion or dark background fills the rest. A narrow cool-white highlight is visible on the actual edge. Retain enough texture to establish glass; do not make a free-floating neon line.
shots.fixed: The pane, edge thickness and its relationship to the frame. The edge stays straight and stationary in the world. Light source and exposure remain fixed. No new panes, particles, dust animation, hand, text or logo.
shots.move: One small rightward camera truck with fixed orientation. Target roughly 6–8% frame-width leftward drift of the edge during the retained two seconds. The background moves less. Let the highlight vary naturally with viewpoint; do not separately animate it upward.
beats: 0–15%: establish the existing illuminated edge; no fade from a different scene.
15–80%: continue one smooth lateral travel. The glass edge remains resolved and rigid; focus does not hunt.
80–100%: a slightly broader steel-blue reflection appears beside the edge because of the new view. End still looking at glass, not at an unrelated building.
shots.finish: Edge near x=50%; the pale-blue reflected area occupies more of the right half. Preserve the same edge thickness. The end should offer a light/dark boundary suitable for the next cut.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic extreme macro along the polished edge of a stationary clear architectural glass pane beside a graphite aluminum frame. The edge is a straight near-vertical line at about three-fifths of the image width, visible from near top to near bottom. Narrow real white reflection on the edge, dark graphite background, restrained steel-blue reflected sky. Material texture and a believable thin edge, fixed focus, clean 16:9 composition. No text, numbering, border, people, floating neon or lens-flare streak. Match the glass and graphite metal of the supplied entrance reference.
shots.prompt: The camera trucks slowly to the right along the fixed polished glass edge. The nearby edge drifts slightly left in the image while the dark background shifts less. A narrow natural reflection changes with the viewing angle. The pane stays rigid and straight. One continuous level move with steady light and fixed focus.
shots.short: Slow rightward camera truck along the stationary glass edge. Gentle parallax, rigid glass, fixed focus and steady light.
shots.timeline: (start: the existing polished glass edge is already visible) (middle: one slow rightward camera truck creates gentle parallax) (end: the edge remains straight beside a slightly wider pale-blue reflection)
shots.reject: A glowing line detached from glass; a bending edge; the pane rotating or sliding by itself; a laser sweep; pulsing exposure; no visible parallax. A digital zoom alone does not meet this shot.
shots.fallback: Keep the geometry almost locked and use an even shorter lateral travel across a clearly visible bevel. If macro material detail is unstable, start at a slightly wider close-up with the frame edge in view. Do not replace it with an abstract graphic and call that photographed glass.
shots.cut: Hard-cut on the pale-blue reflection into shot 02. Align a similar vertical boundary; do not morph the macro edge into a facade.
shots.mobile: Keep the illuminated edge around the center of a separately composed portrait image. Do not crop the edge off-screen simply to preserve the wide composition.

shots.title: Follow the reflection
shots.purpose: Increase the spatial clues. The viewer now sees the exterior world in glass and begins to understand the entrance system.
shots.start: Close oblique view of one stationary glass pane. A graphite mullion stands near x=72%. Steel-blue sky occupies the upper reflected area, one tree is recognizable toward x=40%. A glimpse of the transmitted interior may remain visible; it is not a mirrored metal sheet.
shots.fixed: Glass plane, frame dimensions, tree position in the world and light source. No wind animation for this first pass. No new reflections of people, cars or buildings. The reflected tree may shift optically with camera angle; it must not liquefy or slide as an independent texture.
shots.move: Continue rightward camera translation parallel to the facade. Maintain the same oblique viewing direction; do not add an orbit. Near mullion drifts left roughly 8–12% of the image width in the usable section. Distant reflected detail changes more subtly. Reflection behavior should remain physically plausible rather than satisfy an exact pixel prescription.
beats: 0–15%: recognize the pane, sky and tree without a large focus change.
15–85%: steady rightward truck; the solid mullion provides the motion reference.
85–100%: the dark mullion approaches the center-right cut position. No sudden acceleration or end-frame snap.
shots.finish: The same mullion reaches about x=60–64%; the reflected sky/tree still belong to the same environment. The image remains a close surface study, not a pullback to a whole building.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic close oblique view of the supplied entrance glazing: clear fixed pane, slim graphite vertical mullion toward the right, soft steel-blue sky and one California tree reflected in the pane. Warm lobby remains subtly visible through the glass. Straight mullion, realistic gasket and physically coherent transparent/reflected layers. Neutral whites and graphite, no signs, people, text, border or new architecture. Compose a clean full 16:9 frame with usable near/far depth cues.
shots.prompt: The camera trucks slowly to the right parallel to the stationary glass facade. The nearby graphite mullion moves left across the image while the reflected distant tree changes more gently with the viewing angle. The glass plane and framing remain rigid. Fixed camera orientation, steady daylight, one continuous lateral move.
shots.short: Rightward camera truck beside fixed glazing. The near mullion drifts left; the distant reflection shifts less. Rigid frames, steady light.
shots.timeline: (start: oblique view of sky and a tree reflected in fixed glass) (middle: the camera trucks right and the near mullion drifts left) (end: the same mullion remains straight near center-right)
shots.reject: Reflection swimming like water; a tree growing or multiplying; an orbit that reveals a new facade; sky changing to clouds or night; a stationary camera with only a texture sweep; glass becoming opaque without a viewpoint reason.
shots.fallback: Use a cleaner pane with one strong mullion and a simpler sky reflection. Reduce camera travel before adding controls. If the model cannot maintain transparency, choose a more oblique reference with less visible interior while keeping the material recognizable.
shots.cut: Match the dark mullion to shot 03’s vertical member. Use a direct edit, not an animated transformation from reflection into metal.
shots.mobile: Use a centered mullion and one readable reflected tree. A crop showing only blank blue glass loses the purpose of this shot.

shots.title: Precision at the joint
shots.purpose: Make the trade visible through fit and material. This is also the calibration shot because its simple rigid shapes make deformation easy to detect.
shots.start: Close view of a believable graphite vertical/horizontal framing joint. Vertical member near x=55%; horizontal member crosses near y=60%. A black gasket is visible beside the clear glass. Use consistent member width and realistic meeting geometry.
shots.fixed: All aluminum, joint topology, gasket, screws if already present, glass and lighting. No assembly, extending frame members, tightening screws or sealant being applied. Do not invent a connection detail not visible in the approved keyframe.
shots.move: One short downward camera slide parallel to the fixed vertical member. Because the camera moves down, the horizontal joint should drift upward in the image, roughly y=60% toward y=48–52% in the retained section. No simultaneous focus rack in the base version. Keep the actual frame edges sharp.
beats: 0–15%: static recognition of the joint; focus already on the intended detail.
15–85%: one downward slide. The horizontal feature rises on screen, with a small credible background parallax.
85–100%: settle on the joint/gasket relationship. No new hardware appears when the camera stops.
shots.finish: Same joint, slightly higher on screen; same frame thickness and gasket location. The horizontal seam is a deliberate visual handoff to the threshold in shot 04.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic macro of a real-looking vertical and horizontal graphite aluminum entrance-frame junction matching the common reference. Black gasket seated beside clear glass; subtle metal surface finish, square flush alignment. Vertical member near center-right, horizontal member across the lower middle, clean directional daylight. Sufficient depth of field to see the joint. No tools, hands, labels, logos, numbers, border or decorative hardware.
shots.prompt: The camera slides slowly downward along the fixed vertical aluminum member. The horizontal framing joint rises slightly in the image as the camera descends. The frame width, gasket and glass remain unchanged and rigid. Fixed focus and constant daylight. One short, smooth vertical camera move.
shots.short: Slow downward camera slide past the rigid framing joint. The horizontal seam moves upward on screen. Fixed focus, steady light.
shots.timeline: (start: the framing joint is sharply visible) (middle: the camera slides down, making the horizontal seam rise slightly) (end: the same joint and gasket remain sharp and unchanged)
shots.reject: Frame widening, merging or flexing; gasket becoming a snake-like line; a digital zoom replacing the slide; joint moving downward when the specified camera move should make it rise; autofocus blur hiding instability.
shots.fallback: Use the stable rightward-truck calibration result as an alternate joint shot. Maintain the cut to the horizontal threshold line. A stable simple truck is preferable to a failed vertical move.
shots.cut: Match the joint’s horizontal line to the threshold line at the start of shot 04. Keep the line on a similar vertical portion of the frame so the edit feels deliberate.
shots.mobile: Center the joint and keep both members visible. Do not use a portrait crop that removes the horizontal member and reduces the shot to an unexplained dark stripe.

shots.title: Light at the threshold
shots.purpose: Move from a material detail to the point where outside meets inside. The diagonal daylight becomes the visual direction for entering the building.
shots.start: Very low close view of the real-looking threshold and base of a fixed frame. The horizontal threshold crosses the lower-middle image. Pale terrazzo has a sharp diagonal band of sunlight coming from camera-left. The vertical jamb remains visible near one edge for depth.
shots.fixed: Threshold profile, gasket, floor joint lines, aggregate texture, frame base and sun direction. No wet look, liquid reflections, moving sealant, new dirt or debris. The sun does not travel through hours during this short shot.
shots.move: One short forward push toward the threshold. Keep the lens aimed level-to-slightly-down as established in the keyframe. Target a modest 5–8% apparent increase in a nearby threshold feature, with small floor parallax. Do not lower the camera through the floor or tilt up into the lobby in the same source.
beats: 0–15%: the threshold and diagonal light are already present.
15–85%: gentle forward dolly; near floor details move more than the frame farther ahead.
85–100%: arrive near, but do not collide with, the threshold. Hold the same light and exposure.
shots.finish: A closer, still coherent threshold detail. Leave the diagonal sun stripe visible as a guide into the doorway shot. The camera has not crossed into a different room yet.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic floor-height close-up at the base of the reference graphite entrance. Believable fixed threshold and black seal, clear glass above, pale terrazzo with fine aggregate and straight stable joints. One hard diagonal sunlight stripe enters from outside left. A frame jamb at the edge gives depth. Dry clean materials, restrained reflections, no hands, tools, text, signs or border. Landscape 16:9.
shots.prompt: The low camera makes one short smooth push forward toward the fixed entrance threshold. Nearby terrazzo detail shifts slightly faster than the frame ahead. The threshold, seal and floor joints remain rigid and unchanged. The diagonal sunlight and exposure stay constant. Fixed angle and focus.
shots.short: Short floor-level push toward the fixed threshold. Natural near/far parallax, rigid floor joints and steady sunlight.
shots.timeline: (start: low view of threshold and diagonal sunlight) (middle: a small forward dolly creates floor parallax) (end: a closer stable threshold detail, without crossing the opening)
shots.reject: Floor swimming or stretching; seam moving independent of camera; time-lapse sunlight; camera passing through the sill; sudden tilt into a new interior; extra gasket strands appearing.
shots.fallback: Use a very small lateral slide across the same threshold, with the daylight already fixed in the start frame. Keep all movement within a clearly visible patch of known floor.
shots.cut: The next doorway composition should preserve the diagonal light direction. Cut before any floor-level camera collision, not after it.
shots.mobile: Keep the sill, diagonal light and a piece of the jamb in view. A portrait image of only terrazzo is too abstract at this point in the sequence.

shots.title: A door opens — one action only
shots.purpose: Deliver one unmistakable physical action. Separate door motion from the later camera push so the model does not have to solve both at once.
shots.start: A three-quarter view of the accepted entrance. The active door leaf is already slightly ajar, approximately 15–20 degrees, with its hinge side and handle clearly readable. Pick the leaf and hinge side that actually match the reference. Record that side before generating; do not impose a contradictory new door.
shots.fixed: Camera position, orientation, lens and focus. Facade, opposite leaf, hinge axis, floor and interior light remain fixed. The active leaf retains its rectangular shape; its handle remains attached to the same points. No visible person or new hand.
shots.move: Only the existing active leaf rotates outward a modest additional 10–15 degrees about the fixed hinge axis. It does not translate sideways, scale or change width. The handle traces a short arc with the leaf, not an independent straight-line path. Keep the opening small enough that the hidden side of the door is not a large new invention.
beats: 0–15%: the slightly ajar leaf is already visible; camera is locked.
15–80%: one slow outward hinge rotation. No second opening, recoil or camera move.
80–100%: settle on the slightly wider opening. Other objects and exposure stay unchanged.
shots.finish: Same camera and entrance, active leaf a little farther open. Hinge axis stays in the same image location. The clear doorway is obvious and prepares the next shot, which begins with an already-open door.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic three-quarter view of the common white precast and graphite glass entrance. One existing door leaf is slightly ajar, roughly fifteen to twenty degrees, with a visible plausible hinge attachment and one long stainless pull. Match the reference door count, handle positions, frame divisions and white columns. Warm interior, diagonal daylight on terrazzo, stationary eye-level camera. No people, hands, signs, text or border. Clean 16:9 frame.
shots.prompt: Locked camera. The slightly ajar glass entrance door slowly opens outward a little farther on its existing fixed hinges, then settles. Only that rigid door leaf rotates; its pull handle stays attached. The surrounding frame, other door, floor, camera and lighting remain completely still.
shots.short: Static camera. One existing glass door rotates outward slightly on its fixed hinges. The leaf and attached handle stay rigid. Everything else stays still.
shots.timeline: (start: static camera, existing door slightly ajar) (middle: only that leaf rotates outward through a small arc about its fixed hinge) (end: the door settles a little farther open; camera and building stay fixed)
shots.reject: Sliding door behavior; bending glass; moving hinge axis; floating/duplicated handle; new hands; the opposite leaf moving; camera pushing in; glass changing topology. This shot has a stricter pass gate than the material inserts.
shots.fallback: Use a clean start frame with the door already open and NO door animation. Perform a very small camera-only rightward truck outside the opening. Label this the S05 camera-only fallback. Keep the opening visually readable. Do not spend repeated batches trying to rescue a bad hinge.
shots.cut: Cut while the doorway is clearly open. Shot 06 starts farther along the same clear route, not by flying through a closed pane. Match hinge side and handle count, rather than insisting on an exact frame-for-frame continuous move.
shots.mobile: Keep the active leaf, fixed hinge and central clear passage inside the crop. If both hinge and opening cannot fit, create a dedicated portrait view or use the already-open-door fallback.

shots.title: Cross the clear opening
shots.purpose: The main spatial payoff: the viewer moves from outside into the lobby. It should feel like a short physical dolly, not a teleport or drone tunnel.
shots.start: Camera centered on an already-open, unobstructed doorway. The active leaf is safely away from the path and does not move. A near jamb is visible along one side; a second column and glass office fronts create a deeper background. Camera height is low but not floor-scraping, roughly waist height in visual feel.
shots.fixed: Door leaf, hinges, facade, column spacing, ceiling lights and floor joints. No doors move during this shot. The camera path must stay inside an actual opening visible in the start image. Never pass through a clear glass pane and call it a doorway.
shots.move: One level forward translation into the clear opening. Keep yaw, pitch, roll and focal length fixed. Near jamb expands/drifts toward the outside edge faster than the distant lobby. Use a short travel: enough for obvious near/far parallax and a slight scale increase, without revealing an entire unseen building.
beats: 0–15%: establish the open route and near jamb.
15–85%: smooth forward push. A real jamb may briefly occlude one edge but not wipe the entire screen into a different layout.
85–100%: camera is just inside the threshold, looking into the same room. No sharp turn or acceleration.
shots.finish: A slightly more interior viewpoint; the same floor joints and columns still align. The doorway frame is nearer the sides of the image. The room has not expanded or changed shape.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic view from just outside the common entrance, looking through an existing already-open doorway into the lobby. White square columns and graphite interior office fronts, pale terrazzo floor joints leading straight inside. The open door is fixed safely off the route; a near jamb remains visible at one side for parallax. Warm interior lights and consistent outside-left sunlight. Clean clear path, stable wide-lens perspective without fisheye. No people, text or border.
shots.prompt: The camera makes one smooth short push forward through the already-open clear doorway. The nearby jamb moves outward toward the image edge faster than the distant lobby. The door stays open and motionless. Columns, floor joints and glass framing remain rigid. Level camera, fixed lens, steady light; finish just inside the same entrance.
shots.short: Short level dolly forward through the already-open doorway. Stronger near-jamb parallax, gentler distant-lobby change. Fixed door and rigid building.
shots.timeline: (start: open doorway with a clear path) (middle: the camera pushes straight forward, near jamb drifting toward the edge) (end: just inside the same lobby, with all architecture unchanged)
shots.reject: Camera crossing intact glass; portal morph; growing corridor; floor sliding like a treadmill; perspective zoom without meaningful parallax; a door closing across the path; a newly invented room.
shots.fallback: Stop the camera outside the threshold and use a shorter push. Cut directly to the accepted interior shot 07. A convincing approach plus an edit is stronger than an impossible passage.
shots.cut: Use a naturally passing jamb edge if it exists. Otherwise make a clean hard cut to the interior at a matching level and direction. Do not demand a continuous simulated one-take between incompatible viewpoints.
shots.mobile: The path is centered. The viewer must see it is an opening, with a jamb and floor cue. Keep the leaf away from the cropped central route.

shots.title: The space beyond
shots.purpose: Release the tension of the close-ups with a calm interior view. This shot must be wider and slower than shot 06, with a clear endpoint for the interior sequence.
shots.start: A wide interior showing at least one recognizable white column, graphite glass office fronts on the right and a broad patch of sunlight on the same terrazzo. Camera is already inside and level. Do not add furniture or a different office layout just to fill the frame.
shots.fixed: Column count and position, office-front divisions, ceiling fixtures, floor texture, sun direction and exposure. No doors, people, furnishings or lights move. Glass reflections remain tied to the viewpoint.
shots.move: One restrained sideways camera move to the right, smaller than the preceding forward push. A near column edge drifts left perhaps 3–5% of frame width; the distant office fronts shift less. Fixed focal length and focus. This is not a second corridor fly-through.
beats: 0–15%: the wider room is readable immediately.
15–80%: a slow short lateral drift reveals a little more depth around the fixed column.
80–100%: the movement eases into a nearly still architectural hold. Do not freeze the texture abruptly.
shots.finish: A composed view of the same glass office fronts and sunlit floor. The room remains stable. There is room in the edit to feel a short visual pause before the exterior cut.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic wide interior of the same white commercial lobby. Recognizable square white columns, graphite glass office fronts to the right, pale terrazzo and warm linear ceiling lights. One defined afternoon sunlight patch from outside-left. Restrained level architectural camera and straight verticals, enough depth around a near column for small parallax. No people, new furniture, labels, logo, text or border. Landscape 16:9.
shots.prompt: Inside the lobby, the camera makes a very short slow truck to the right, then eases toward a calm hold. The nearby white column drifts slightly left while the distant glass office fronts shift less. The room, framing, floor joints and lighting remain unchanged. Level view and fixed lens; no forward fly-through.
shots.short: Very slow short rightward truck inside the fixed lobby. Gentle near-column parallax, then a calm hold. Rigid architecture and steady daylight.
shots.timeline: (start: wide stable interior with glass office fronts) (middle: a small rightward camera truck reveals depth around a fixed column) (end: settle on the same sunlit room)
shots.reject: Indistinguishable from shot 06; office fronts assembling themselves; new furniture/people; breathing columns; sliding sunlight; a zoom into a completely different office.
shots.fallback: Use a locked-off interior with one naturally reflective depth cue and a deliberate short hold. Label it as a hold; do not claim camera motion. The edit still needs a different shot size from 06.
shots.cut: Direct intentional cut to the exterior at blue hour. A time-of-day and viewpoint change is allowed here. Do not dissolve incompatible columns together.
shots.mobile: Prioritize a near column edge and the glass office front; preserve floor depth. If a crop hides both features, compose a new portrait keyframe.

shots.title: The entrance, resolved
shots.purpose: A clean final architectural view with warm light behind the glazing. The door and frame are now part of a complete place. This supplies a strong poster candidate and an honest ending.
shots.start: Wide three-quarter exterior of the SAME entrance at blue hour, prepared as its own clean still. Keep reference columns, opening proportions, mullion pattern and handle count. Interior is already warmly lit. The sky and facade are fully established at the start; no day-to-night transformation.
shots.fixed: Entire building, entrance leaves, lights, planting and sky illumination. No new upper story, additional bays, illuminated signage or changing landscaping. Do not fabricate a specific client building.
shots.move: One short slow pullback along the existing view direction. No orbit, tilt or rising drone move. The entrance becomes only modestly smaller, roughly 5–8% in apparent height across the retained range. Near planting, if present, may separate through parallax; the facade must remain rigid.
beats: 0–15%: already blue hour with steady warm interior light.
15–80%: restrained pullback; the same entrance remains the unmistakable focus.
80–100%: ease toward a clean final hold. Leave a stable poster frame. Do not force a dark wipe unless a real fixed foreground mullion actually exists in the accepted source.
shots.finish: The same entrance held cleanly with warm interior light and steel-blue exterior. No written end card inside the generated scene. The website headline and CTA remain HTML.
shots.keyframe: Photorealistic wide three-quarter exterior at blue hour of the entrance from the supplied reference. Same white precast square columns, graphite mullion pattern, clear glass leaves and stainless pulls, warm linear interior lighting. Pale steel-blue sky and restrained California planting. Building proportions and opening counts match the accepted day reference. Clean dry architecture, no signs, people, vehicles, logo, border or added story. 16:9 composition with the entrance clearly framed.
shots.prompt: At blue hour, the camera makes a short slow pullback from the existing glass entrance and eases into a stable final view. The entrance becomes slightly smaller with natural depth parallax. The white facade, graphite frames, doors, planting and warm interior lights remain fixed and unchanged. No orbit or time-lapse.
shots.short: Slow short pullback from the fixed blue-hour entrance, then hold. Steady warm interior lights, rigid facade, no time-of-day change.
shots.timeline: (start: finished entrance already at blue hour) (middle: one restrained straight pullback) (end: a clean stable wide hold of the same building)
shots.reject: Different facade or door count; daylight suddenly changing; rapidly switching lights; drone lift or spinning orbit; melted frame divisions; a generated CGC logo; a fake customer sign.
shots.fallback: A fixed wide ending with no generated camera move, or a slightly closer already-accepted entrance angle with a tiny pullback. Preserve identity over spectacle. Label any hold in the edit log.
shots.cut: For the main edit, end cleanly on the wide view. Test a match cut back to 01 separately. If there is no matching dark edge, keep an intentional loop cut or produce the optional closing insert after acceptance; do not invent a looping camera teleport.
shots.mobile: Show the entrance and one recognizable white column, not the whole facade squeezed into portrait. Preserve warm interior detail and a stable place for the website crop.
